Class 5 · Chapter 9 of 10

Charts, averages and true statements

Read the scale, combine results and justify a claim.

  1. See it
  2. Try it
  3. Practise it
  4. Print it
  5. Check it

This chapter works best after Plan a budget and compare value. You can still look around, or jump to the check.

By the end I can…

  • I can read pictographs and scaled bars.
  • I can compare two displays or a line graph.
  • I can find an average and check a chart statement.

1 See it

Screen 1 of 4

Pictograph keys

Read the key first. Here each ● is 5 crates.

Count the symbols, then multiply by 5.

Four symbols mean 20 crates.

Screen 2 of 4

Unusual scales

Check the numbers up the side before you read a bar.

If each gridline is 20, a bar halfway between 40 and 60 is 50.

Never assume the scale counts by 1.

Screen 3 of 4

The mean

Four outposts collected 12, 14, 10 and 16 samples.

Total: 12 + 14 + 10 + 16 = 52. Divide by 4.

The mean is 13. If every outpost had the same, each would have 13.

Screen 4 of 4

Check a statement

Read the claim. Then test it with the bars.

Find each value and compare it to the claim.

A claim is true only if the numbers match every time.

Words to know
key
The note that tells you what each symbol or step stands for.
scale
How much each step on an axis is worth.
mean
The average. Add all the values, then divide by how many there are.
line graph
A graph that joins points to show change over time.

For parents

What your child learns

A key tells what one symbol or one gridline stands for. If a gridline is every 12, count in 12s. To compare, find the largest and smallest values and subtract.

A common slip

Children often assume each line is 1 or 10. Read the scale first. Then multiply the count by the key value.

5-minute home activity: Key reading

  1. Draw a pictograph where one symbol means 4 crates.
  2. Show 5 outposts with different symbol counts.
  3. Read each value using the key.
  4. Find the difference between the biggest and smallest.
